title: The Latest in Literacy: 5/19/26
author: Karen Vaites
summary: A curated literacy roundup with editorial synthesis across reading research, curriculum policy, and ed tech. Key threads: a Stanford report declared a 'reading recession,' the RAND report on books in ELA is being misread (Doug Lemov's book-rich curriculum doesn't qualify as 'standards-aligned' due to market failures), the field can't agree on what counts as curriculum quality, and parent backlash against ed tech is intensifying in Lower Merion and against iReady.
points: Stanford Educational Opportunity Project report declared a 'reading recession' — viral NYT graphic drew 2.5M views showing declining reading scores.
Florida's reading declines traced to over-reliance on basals and technology rather than complete books; Florida is 'awash in basals' per Vaites.

RAND report on books in ELA: Doug Lemov's Reading Reconsidered — a genuinely exemplary, book-rich curriculum — doesn't qualify as 'standards-aligned' and appears on zero state-approved lists due to market failures.
Curriculum confusion: the field can't agree on what counts as curriculum quality, or even what counts as curriculum — a red flag against blanket curriculum mandates.
New study: more time spent on phonics was associated with lower DIBELS scores; more time on comprehension linked with higher standardized test scores.
Lower Merion parent backlash: 600+ signatures on petition to opt out of devices; coverage has shifted from local to national.
iReady backlash: a school board VP reports she has 'yet to hear a positive comment' from district educators — dozens of parents burst into applause.
Teens are Night Owl Scrolling: JAMA Pediatrics data shows U.S. adolescents average 50 minutes of smartphone use on school nights, with over half scrolling midnight to 4am.
quotes: Reform done poorly is often worse than no reform at all. —Rick Hess
Market failures are keeping exemplary, book-rich curricula off state lists in favor of basals, and that's the elephant in the room.
